problems.description: 8 convention violations (convention score 0.73): PascalCase for classes, snake_case for functions, and UPPER_CASE module-level constants violated across app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, and test_app.py.
Session 1 drops the seed's entire auth/JWT + Blueprint layer wholesale; while a task CRUD story doesn't require auth, later sessions may need to re-add it, incurring rework.
init_db() runs as a module-import side effect in app.py, coupling DB schema creation to import time rather than an app-context or factory.

strengths: Keeps the established Flask + SQLite stack and pytest test layout from the seed, preserving the repo's technology patterns.
Input validation with proper 400 responses on missing/blank title, and consistent JSON response shapes across endpoints.
Multi-file structure (repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) rather than a monolithic app.py, respecting modular organization.
Truncated diff's -184/+142 net reduction shows the agent removed unused scaffolding, keeping the baseline lean for a greenfield session.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound session-1 greenfield baseline that delivers working CRUD on the existing Flask/SQLite stack with only style-level convention violations (0.73), though it abandons the seed's auth layer and modular structure wholesale.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT/HMAC auth (base64url + hmac) instead of a maintained library like PyJWT/Flask-JWT-Extended — custom token validation is a security surface even though the implementation is correct (compare_digest, exp check, signature-before-decode).
SECRET_KEY silently falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key'; if deployed without the env var set, all tokens become forgeable.

Mechanical convention score 0.73 with 8 violations, but most are in untouched pre-existing files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py); the diff itself follows snake_case/UPPER_CASE consistently — flagged as a measurement vs. qualitative-judgment discrepancy.
Schema evolution (ALTER TABLE owner_id) is inline in init_db rather than a versioned migration mechanism; pragmatic for this scale but unstructured.

strengths: Owner_id scoping on every task query (list/get/update) enforces per-user data isolation, not just authentication.
Constant-time signature comparison via hmac.compare_digest and an exp claim check — the manual crypto is done correctly.
Zero new runtime dependencies (stdlib hmac/hashlib/base64 + werkzeug already present via Flask).
Tests updated with a register helper so authenticated flows are covered.
Naming and style (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants, existing error-response shape) stay consistent with the file.
commit_reviews.summary: Cleanly retrofits per-user JWT auth with owner-scoped queries and updated tests, but the mechanical 0.73 convention score is driven mostly by violations in files this commit did not touch, and the hand-rolled token implementation introduces a security-surface/maintainability debt that would be better served by a maintained auth library.

problems.description: celery_config.py hardcodes BROKER_URL/RESULT_BACKEND to localhost:6379 instead of reading from environment variables; the framework queue lives on port 6380, so hardcoding 6379 is only safe by accident of the story-agent isolation.

send_notification_email.delay is fired before the DB transaction is committed, so a notification can be dispatched for a task update that later rolls back (no atomicity between the side effect and the commit).
Notification dispatch logic is embedded directly in the update_task route handler rather than extracted to a service layer, coupling business side effects to the HTTP layer.
Tests hardcode resource id /tasks/1, which is fragile if the sqlite DB persists across tests and ids advance.

Most of the 8 SonarQube violations (Classes should use PascalCase in app.py/tasks.py/test_app.py, repositories.py Module-level constants) are pre-existing repo-wide style flags, not introduced by this diff; the new files actually use UPPER_CASE constants (BROKER_URL, RESULT_BACKEND). The 0.73 mechanical score understates this commit's own adherence.

strengths: Clean separation of the Celery app into its own celery_config.py with task routing to an email queue.
Follows the existing migration pattern (PRAGMA column check + ALTER TABLE) for adding users.email.
Three focused tests cover trigger on completion, no-trigger on other statuses, and idempotency on repeat completion.
Graceful fallback when owner email is missing; mock sender keeps the story deterministic and testable.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-respecting addition that cleanly decouples async email notifications via Celery, with only minor config-hardcoding and transaction-ordering concerns.

problems.description: BaseRepository interpolates identifiers (table_name, column names) into SQL via f-strings in get_by_id/all/create/update. Values are parameterized and identifiers currently come from subclass constants / caller kwarg keys, so it is not exploitable today, but it is a latent SQL-injection footgun if any column name ever flows from request data.

The new repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository + BaseRepository) is added with no new tests in this commit; the diff only touches app.py and repositories.py, so the refactor moves untested SQL into a new module.

update_task now does the ownership check (get_by_owner_and_id) and the mutation (update_task) on separate connections/statements instead of inside one connection as before, slightly widening a TOCTOU window; low risk but a regression from the original single-connection flow.

Mechanical measurement flags repositories.py for 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' (8 total violations, convention score 0.73); the other 7 violations are in files untouched by this diff (app.py, celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) and are pre-existing, so the score overstates what this commit introduced.

strengths: Centralizes all SQLite access in a repository layer so route handlers no longer touch SQL directly — a clean separation-of-concerns improvement.
Removes the duplicated ownership-scoped query pattern previously repeated in get_task/update_task via get_by_owner_and_id.
Respects existing patterns: reuses the get_db connection factory/context manager, preserves Flask route structure, decorators, response shapes, and status codes (404/400/409/401 all intact).
Behavior-preserving refactor: error handling and notification logic carried over unchanged, with a PascalCase/snake_case style consistent with the codebase.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving repository-layer refactor that centralizes SQL and eliminates duplicated queries, introducing only minor debt from generic f-string-built SQL and an untested new module — the 0.73 convention score is largely carried by pre-existing violations in untouched files, which I flag as a discrepancy with the 'introduced' framing.

problems.description: Measured convention score is 0.73 with 8 violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE in app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) — but the AST diff adds no classes and only snake_case functions/imports, so these violations are pre-existing repo-wide debt, not introduced by this commit.
Dead code in list_tasks: `if limit is None: limit = 20` is unreachable because request.args.get already supplies default=20 (and type=int conversion).
list_by_owner_paginated runs a full COUNT(*) over owner tasks on every page — O(n) per request; acceptable at this scale but could be avoided if total is not needed on each page.

RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379 and configure_limiter() runs at import time; if redis is unavailable in a non-test deploy the limiter init will fail. Tests correctly override to memory://.

strengths: User-scoped rate-limit keys (auth 'sub') with IP fallback — better isolation than a global or IP-only key
Keyset pagination (id < cursor, ORDER BY id DESC, fetch limit+1) avoids OFFSET deep-pagination cost and is stable under writes
Sane caps enforced (default 20, max 100) and consistent env-var config pattern matching the existing DATABASE/SECRET_KEY style
Comprehensive test coverage: pagination walk-through, default limit, 100 cap, owner isolation, and 429 retry-after; existing tests updated to the new response envelope
Test fixture cleanly isolates the limiter via memory:// storage plus reset(), keeping tests deterministic
commit_reviews.summary: A clean cross-cutting session that adds user-scoped rate limiting and keyset pagination following the repository/env-var patterns with strong test coverage, where the measured 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing repo-wide style debt rather than this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1 rewrote the seed as raw-sqlite3 CRUD and never used SQLAlchemy; the spec constraints (categories, priorities, due dates, search/filter by status/category/priority) were silently dropped, so sessions 2-5 layered features onto a schema that structurally lacks the required fields.

Session 2 replaced the seed's entropy-based secret (`secrets.token_hex(32)`) with a hardcoded `SECRET_KEY = "dev-secret-key"` default that persisted through to the final commit, leaving a known-insecure default in the shipped code.

The convention violations inherited from the seed (score stuck at 0.733 across all sessions) were never fixed even in the dedicated refactor session 4, which restructured modules but left naming violations in app.py, tasks.py, and test_app.py untouched.

Session 5's flask_limiter is configured with a hard redis://localhost:6379 storage default and configure_limiter() runs at import time, introducing an unconditional external runtime dependency on module load.

Module-level `init_db()` at import time couples schema migration to importing app.py; tests only work because the fixture re-runs init_db() against a temp path and the CREATE/ALTER guards are idempotent.
key_decisions: Session 1 greenfield rewrite: repurposed the seed auth/items API into a tasks-only Flask+SQLite CRUD app (dropped the seed's JWT scaffolding, blueprints, and multi-table design).
Session 2 added a hand-rolled HS256 JWT implementation (hmac/base64, no PyJWT) with werkzeug password hashing and per-user task ownership via a migration-added `owner_id` column.
Session 3 integrated Celery with a Redis broker to fire a mocked `send_notification_email` async task on task completion, adding an `email` column to users.
Session 4 extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) so route handlers no longer touch SQL directly.
Session 5 added flask_limiter rate limiting (per-user via token subject, IP fallback) plus keyset cursor pagination with total-count and capped limits on the list endpoint.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean but minimal CRUD skeleton; session 2 materially improved it with real JWT auth, hashed passwords, and owner-scoped data isolation; session 3 added a sensible async notification seam; session 4 genuinely de-risked the code by introducing a repository pattern that removed raw SQL from route handlers; session 5 rounded it out with rate limiting, proper pagination, and a test suite that grew from ~10 to 26 tests covering security and edge cases. All 5 sessions passed their tests (test_executed_success=True, 897s total, $0.09, 95.8% cache hit). The arc is structurally upward — each session built on the prior one's interfaces — but it delivered a functional subset of the spec (no categories, priorities, due dates, or search/filter), and the refactor session missed the chance to clear long-standing convention violations and the insecure default secret.
story_review.summary: A coherent and improving 5-session arc (build → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening) that produced a working, well-tested task API, but quietly shed the spec's category/priority/due-date/search constraints in session 1 and never recovered them, leaving the final deliverable as a solid but narrower-than-required app.
